claims.text: A model using temperature-dependent ab initio force constants and electron-phonon scattering rates can separately compute lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The model will predict the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr within 15% of experimental values over 200–1200 K.
The model will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 20–30% relative to previous approaches.
The target HfNbTaTiZr material is near equilibrium, has minimal defects, and contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen or less.
The proposed model includes DFT-derived force constants and electron-scattering parameters.
Model applicability requires specimens without significant secondary phases and with no more than 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen atoms perturb the lattice and act as minor defect sites in HfNbTaTiZr.
Separating lattice and electronic conductive channels allows the temperature dependence of each contribution to be independently refined.
Earlier perfect-crystal approximations using Debye-temperature-based estimates conflated lattice and electronic transport.
Decoupling lattice and electronic transport will capture the experimentally observed complexity more accurately than earlier approaches.
Recombining the separately predicted lattice and electronic contributions will improve agreement with measured total thermal conductivity by 20–30%.

Existing analytical and simulation approaches generally assume perfect, defect-free crystals and approximate combined lattice-electronic transport, often with a single Debye-temperature approximation.
Existing approaches have shown discrepancies relative to experimental thermal-conductivity data.
Outside 200–1200 K or above 1 wt.% oxygen, additional structural complexity or defect scattering may reduce predictive accuracy.
Atomistic data on temperature-dependent electron-phonon interactions in complex HfNbTaTiZr are limited.
Approximately ±10% uncertainty may remain in the model predictions.
Isotope labeling, magnetic-field selective scattering, or ion irradiation can be used to isolate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity channels in this alloy.
